2611.21559.tldr: Reference Forcing reduces drift in autoregressive long video generation by distilling a region-masked attention teacher into an anchor attention path on initial frames, and by correcting drifted KV-cache values toward matching initial-frame values. It reports best consistency among long-video methods.
2611.21559.why: Directly relevant to efficient autoregressive video diffusion with KV caches and attention sinks (LongLive-style); the region-level anchoring and value correction ideas may transfer to world-model rollouts.
2611.21559.reason: Long video AR generation with KV cache and distillation; strongly matches core interests
2611.21559.qn: Sensible, targeted fix with ablations; evidence is mostly VBench-style consistency metrics.
2611.21559.abs: Long video generation should keep the subject and background consistent while supporting rich, natural motion. However, autoregressive models are often distilled with distribution matching distillation (DMD) over short windows, which does not train them to keep this consistency over long ranges. As a result, the subject and background can drift over time. Methods that manage the key-value (KV) cache retain or retrieve history to reduce drift. Yet this history may itself have drifted. We propose Reference Forcing, which uses the initial frames as an appearance reference. We first build a teacher that uses attention masks to force each region of a new frame to attend to the same region in the initial frames. The teacher finds these regions with off-the-shelf segmentation models. We then distill this behavior into a separate attention path of the student, which needs no external models at inference. We further introduce value correction, which corrects drifted values in the KV cache toward the matching values of drift-free initial frames. Experiments show that Reference Forcing achieves state-of-the-art subject and background consistency among long-video methods on different base models, and its advantage grows with video length. Ablations show both components are needed to gain consistency without losing motion. More visualizations and code are available at https://zhaosheng-thu.github.io/reference-force/

2611.20307.tldr: Training-free sparse attention for video DiTs: offline-calibrated relative-offset positional tables supply stable keys, online selection adds content keys with per-head ratios, pooled virtual keys compensate the rest, and a step-wise budget is front-loaded. Reports 1.9–5.0 dB PSNR gains and 4.1× attention speedup.
2611.20307.why: Directly targets efficient inference for video diffusion transformers via sparse attention; the offset-based positional prior and step-adaptive budget are practical ideas to build on or compare against.
2611.20307.reason: Sparse attention acceleration for video diffusion transformers, a core interest
2611.20307.qn: Sensible decomposition with broad models and tasks; incremental over existing sparse attention.
2611.20307.abs: Video diffusion transformers rely on 3D full attention over tens of thousands of spatiotemporal tokens, and its quadratic cost dominates inference latency. Sparse attention reduces this cost, but existing methods face a dilemma: static methods apply predefined masks and cannot capture input-dependent attention, whereas dynamic methods reconstruct the sparse mask repeatedly, paying online to rediscover positional structure that is largely stable across inputs. To this end, we propose PoCoAttn, a training-free sparse attention framework that separates input-stable from input-dependent attention and resolves the former offline and the latter online. PoCoAttn features: (1) A relative-offset analysis of 3D query-key pairs, which shows that video attention decomposes into an input-stable positional prior that carries most of the attention mass and a small content-dependent residual. (2) A position-content collaborative sparse attention mechanism, which retrieves positional keys from offline-calibrated tables, selects content keys online with a head-adaptive ratio between the two sources, and compensates for the discarded keys to approximate full attention. (3) A step-adaptive budget allocation algorithm, which models how early-step sparse attention errors are amplified along the denoising trajectory and derives the optimal sparsity budget per step. Extensive experiments across four video diffusion models and three tasks show that PoCoAttn consistently achieves a better speed-fidelity Pareto frontier than state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, improving PSNR by 1.9 to 5.0 dB over baselines and delivering up to 4.1$\times$ attention and 2.0$\times$ denoising speedups over dense FlashAttention-3 attention.

2611.21339.tldr: MovieRoll is a streaming long-video pipeline: window-wise teacher forcing, hierarchical KV-cache compression (up to 78% memory cut), and gradient-averaged long-rollout DMD distillation. It tops HeliosBench totals up to 60s among compared methods.
2611.21339.why: It bundles streaming video DiT work: KV-cache compression, few-step DMD distillation, and long-horizon extrapolation. All are directly relevant to efficient, consistent video world models.
2611.21339.reason: Streaming long-video generation with KV compression and distillation; core topic
2611.21339.qn: Many engineering components; gains plausible but evidence is bundled and benchmark-specific.
2611.21339.abs: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.

2611.19857.tldr: PanDWM stitches six driving cameras into one 360° panorama, generates it with a 4-step causal student distilled from a 50-step teacher and trained on its own rollouts, then lifts frames to 3D/4D Gaussians feed-forward; reports better FID/FVD at 8-46× speed.
2611.19857.why: Combines few-step causal video diffusion distillation with feed-forward Gaussian lifting for world models, which touches efficient video DiT inference, 4D reconstruction and 3D-consistent generation.
2611.19857.reason: Panoramic 4D driving world model with distillation and 3D Gaussians; squarely core.
2611.19857.qn: Sensible integration, but evaluation is on nuScenes only and FID/FVD is scored in a stitched view.
2611.19857.abs: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.

2611.21302.tldr: Distills a recurrent shared-block RGB feed-forward 3D model (Déjà View) into an event-only student by matching final tokens, training ~1% of parameters. Adds per-patch event-density gating; halves DSEC AbsRel (0.15 vs 0.30) with ~1/10 the parameters of EventVGGT.
2611.21302.why: Feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction (VGGT-style) extended to a new modality via token distillation; the recurrent shared-block refinement and adaptive gating are relevant to efficient transformer design.
2611.21302.reason: Feed-forward multi-view geometry from event cameras via distillation; close to core
2611.21302.qn: Sensible distillation with strong zero-shot gains, but niche modality and a limited set of baselines.
2611.21302.abs: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present D\'ej\`a-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from D\'ej\`a View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, D\'ej\`a-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

2611.18708.tldr: TopSDF models tetrahedral-grid SDF values as a Gaussian random field with learned covariances, solved in closed form via RKHS, and adds meshing energies plus energy-guided Gaussian densification. It reports +0.86 dB mesh-based PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360 and aspect ratio improved from 0.37 to 0.49.
2611.18708.why: Mesh extraction from 3DGS via marching tetrahedra is directly relevant to optimization-based 3D reconstruction; the topological SDF and mesh-quality energies could improve downstream mesh pipelines.
2611.18708.reason: Mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting, directly in core 3DGS interest
2611.18708.qn: Plausible gains on standard benchmarks; theoretical claims and baseline strength unclear from introduction.
2611.18708.abs: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated its effectiveness for photorealistic novel view synthesis. However, extracting clean, watertight, explicit surface meshes from 3DGS remains a critical challenge. Previous methods approximate geometry via discrete Marching Tetrahedra, where each grid vertex is assigned a single scalar signed distance value. At complex geometric boundaries and thin structures, this suboptimal parameterization forces severe compromises across shared vertices, causing gradient collisions and geometric frustration. Furthermore, existing optimization objectives neglect element shape conditioning, producing degenerate triangles. We introduce TopSDF, a framework that models the signed distance state as a multivariate Gaussian random field. By learning latent topological covariances across tetrahedral vertices, our formulation expands local degrees of freedom for SDF estimates, allowing the candidate mesh vertices to be placed flexibly along the bipolar edges in the tetrahedra as driven by such topological correlation. Concurrently, we directly integrate variational meshing energies into the joint optimization, coupled with an energy-driven Gaussian densification strategy to improve triangle mesh quality. Our experiments across Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and ScanNet++ show that TopSDF achieves state-of-the-art mesh-based novel view rendering (+0.86 dB PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360) and triangle-mesh quality (from 0.37 to 0.49 aspect ratio).

2611.21038.tldr: Training-free acceleration for few-step autoregressive video diffusion (Self-Forcing, LongLive): predicts an intermediate denoising update from shallow features, allocates per-head historical KV budgets, and sparsifies cache construction. Reports 1.86–2.28× speedups with small quality gains on VBench and MovieGen.
2611.21038.why: Directly targets efficient inference for video diffusion transformers (caching, sparse attention, KV reading) in autoregressive world-model-style long video generation; a practical toolbox for your efficiency work.
2611.21038.reason: Efficient few-step autoregressive video diffusion with KV caching; core interest.
2611.21038.qn: Sensible combined engineering; speedups modest, quality gains from training-free skipping are suspicious.
2611.21038.abs: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.

2611.20461.tldr: LiveView distills a bidirectional camera-controlled video-to-video teacher into a few-step causal autoregressive student for streaming re-filming, using Cross-Frame Injection, Shared Relative RoPE and Cycle Streaming Tuning for long-horizon stability.
2611.20461.why: Combines camera-controlled video generation, few-step causal distillation and RoPE handling for long rollouts, directly relevant to world models and efficient video diffusion transformers.
2611.20461.reason: Camera-controlled video re-filming with few-step distillation and RoPE; close to core
2611.20461.qn: Sensible engineering combination; novelty is incremental and the intro excerpt shows no evidence.
2611.20461.abs: Real-time camera-controlled video re-filming aims to synthesize target views from a streaming source video under online user-specified camera trajectories. This task poses two key challenges: maintaining synchronization and content consistency across views, and achieving low-latency rendering with long-horizon stability. Existing approaches are predominantly designed for offline full-sequence processing and rely on bidirectional attention or costly depth-based geometric preprocessing, making them unsuitable for low-latency streaming scenarios. To address these limitations, we develop a teacher-to-student framework that distills a high-fidelity bidirectional re-filming teacher into a few-step causal autoregressive student. We introduce Cross-Frame Injection to interleave each incoming source frame with its synchronized target latent, thereby establishing direct cross-view correspondence and improving content consistency. To ensure stable long-horizon generation, we further propose Shared Relative RoPE, which bounds temporal indices within the pretrained range, and Cycle Streaming Tuning, which exposes the student to extended cyclic trajectories during streaming training. These designs enable low-latency online video re-filming with precise camera control and sustained spatiotemporal consistency over long streaming rollouts.

2611.19822.tldr: FlipTest probes video world models with minimal-pair initial frames whose true futures differ across a physical boundary; all 11 models score below chance (best 18.3% vs 25%), flip equally on control steps, while VLMs and coding agents localize the boundary.
2611.19822.why: Directly challenges the assumption that video diffusion world models learn scene state; offers a counterfactual benchmark relevant to evaluating world models and physical consistency in video generation.
2611.19822.reason: Probes whether video world models track world state; relevant to world-model evaluation.
2611.19822.qn: Clever counterfactual benchmark with diagnostics; outcome-classification protocol and 'below chance' framing may depend on judging method.
2611.19822.abs: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.

2611.21126.tldr: IGRecon4D is a feed-forward 4D Gaussian driving-scene reconstructor that distills instance-segmentation priors into dynamic-mask learning and anchors Gaussians with LiDAR-guided depth. It improves Waymo reconstruction and zero-shot nuScenes results on traffic-participant regions.
2611.21126.why: It is a feed-forward 4D Gaussian reconstruction method with dynamic/static decomposition, directly in your core area. Its LiDAR-anchored positioning and mask distillation are ideas to borrow or compare against.
2611.21126.reason: Feed-forward 4D Gaussian driving reconstruction with dynamic-object handling; core topic
2611.21126.qn: Sensible incremental fixes for DGGT-style pipelines; novelty and gains appear modest.
2611.21126.abs: Feed-forward 4D driving-scene reconstruction enables efficient modeling of dynamic autonomous-driving scenes, but current methods suffer from two complementary failure modes: semantic leakage of traffic participants into the static representation and geometric drift of Gaussian locations across viewpoints. We propose \textbf{IGRecon4D}, a feed-forward dynamic scene reconstruction framework that addresses these failures with training-time instance-prior distillation and LiDAR-anchored Gaussian positioning. Specifically, an instance-level semantic branch provides a potentially dynamic participant prior, which is distilled into dynamic-mask learning through the Instance-Dynamic Consistency Constraint to encourage high-recall localization of traffic-participant regions prone to dynamic-static leakage. In parallel, sparse LiDAR measurements guide dense depth estimation, and the resulting depths are back-projected to anchor Gaussian positions for improved multi-view geometric consistency. Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and zero-shot evaluation on nuScenes demonstrate improved full-image reconstruction on the main benchmark and stronger traffic-participant-region reconstruction under cross-dataset evaluation.

2611.20703.tldr: Global-Local Proxy Attention keeps full-resolution within-view attention and uses pooled global proxies for cross-view exchange, refined iteratively within a denoising step. On FLUX it gives 2.65× attention speedup with IoU 0.685→0.702; on SD it gives 1.80×.
2611.20703.why: It targets efficient cross-view attention in multi-view diffusion for 3D reconstruction, which is relevant to sparse attention and efficient multi-view generation. The proxy-token idea could carry over to video DiTs.
2611.20703.reason: Efficient cross-view attention for multi-view diffusion, close to 3D generation and attention efficiency
2611.20703.qn: Sensible efficiency idea, modest gains, narrow benchmarks, limited novelty over token-reduction methods.
2611.20703.abs: Generating consistent multi-view RGB images and normal maps from a single input image provides complementary appearance and geometric cues for 3D reconstruction. However, maintaining cross-view consistency requires information exchange across viewpoints, and dense cross-view attention becomes computationally expensive as the number of views and spatial resolution increase. In this paper, we propose Global-Local Proxy Attention (GLPA) to reduce cross-view communication costs while preserving fine-grained within-view processing. Specifically, GLPA retains full-resolution interactions within each view and uses compact global proxies for cross-view communication. To further leverage the exchanged information, GLPA incorporates iterative proxy refinement, which rebuilds the proxies from updated features and reuses the same attention parameters for subsequent interactions within a single denoising step. We evaluate GLPA on two structurally different diffusion backbones, FLUX and Stable Diffusion. Experiments on FLUX show that GLPA achieves a $2.65\times$ speedup in attention computation per denoising step over dense attention, while improving reconstruction IoU from 0.6849 to 0.7019 and reducing NVS LPIPS from 0.086 to 0.076. Results on Stable Diffusion further demonstrate the effectiveness of GLPA, with a $1.80\times$ attention speedup and improvements across all five quality metrics.

2611.21479.tldr: Hand-controlled video world model trained on 100K interaction clips, with hand-aware losses, a 3-step causal flow-map student using region-aware dual-score distillation, and a fast VAE decoder; reaches 18 FPS at 540p on an H200, 92.49 MANO Dice.
2611.21479.why: Combines camera-conditioned video DiT world models with few-step causal distillation and fast decoding, directly relevant to efficient interactive video generation, though hand control itself is peripheral.
2611.21479.reason: Hand-controlled video world model with few-step distillation and fast decoder
2611.21479.qn: Solid engineering pipeline, but a mostly incremental combination of known techniques; the introduction shows limited ablation evidence.
2611.21479.abs: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

2611.21253.tldr: Post-hoc method for frozen 3DGS: two per-Gaussian attributes predict lower/upper RGB-MAE quantiles, then scale-normalized conformal calibration yields error bounds. At 90% target, coverage rises from 69.6% to 89.6% on LLFF and 80.1% to 92.1% on Mip-NeRF 360.
2611.21253.why: Calibrated per-pixel error bounds for 3DGS could support view selection, pruning, and SLAM, and may guide reconstruction-quality assessment in 3D/4D pipelines.
2611.21253.reason: Conformal uncertainty bounds for 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering; strongly relevant
2611.21253.qn: Sound conformal setup, but pixel exchangeability is questionable and the guarantee is only marginal.
2611.21253.abs: Uncertainty quantification for novel view synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assesses rendering reliability at unseen viewpoints. This reliability depends on the discrepancy between rendered and true colors, which cannot be measured without ground-truth images. We therefore quantify uncertainty in this unknown discrepancy through upper bounds on per-pixel RGB mean absolute error. However, learned bounds may underestimate these errors and overstate rendering reliability, motivating calibration to a prescribed coverage level. In this paper, we propose QuantileGS, a post-hoc framework that combines learned rendering-error quantiles with scale-normalized conformal calibration to produce spatially adaptive error bounds. The framework comprises three phases. Phase 1, Rendering-Error Computation, measures RGB mean absolute error between observed images and predictions from a frozen 3DGS model. Phase 2, Ordered Gaussian Quantile Fields, learns two scalar attributes per Gaussian to predict lower and upper rendering-error quantiles. Phase 3, Scale-Normalized Conformal Calibration, calibrates the upper prediction on held-out images, using the quantile gap to scale the correction. Under the stated assumptions, the resulting bounds provide finite-sample marginal coverage. At a nominal coverage level of 90%, calibration raises mean empirical test coverage from 69.6% to 89.6% on LLFF and from 80.1% to 92.1% on Mip-NeRF 360. On LF, coverage remains conservative at 96.3% before and 96.4% after calibration. Applications to active view selection, Gaussian pruning, and RGB-D simultaneous localization and mapping illustrate how these bounds inform downstream decisions.

2611.20704.tldr: Training-free sparse attention for DiT video editing that sets per-query, per-key-source sparsity using a risk proxy (attention mass plus intra-block score dispersion). Reports up to 1.46x end-to-end speedup on three editors and 1.36x on reference-to-video.
2611.20704.why: It is efficient inference for video DiTs via sparse attention, a core interest. The per-source adaptive sparsity idea could carry over to camera- or reference-conditioned generation.
2611.20704.reason: Sparse attention acceleration for video diffusion transformers, a core interest
2611.20704.qn: Sensible but incremental over Sol-Attn/SPADE/ISA; modest speedups, narrow application.
2611.20704.abs: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong performance in generation based video editing, but suffer from high inference latency due to the long token sequences formed by conditioning inputs and generated videos. Although training-free sparse attention reduces this cost, existing methods typically apply a fixed retention ratio or a single threshold shared across all tokens. In this work, we view video editing as conditional generation and identify a key insight: attention demand varies significantly both across different key sources (e.g., source videos, reference images, audio, text, and generated videos) and across queries within each source. Motivated by this, we propose QASK-Edit (Query-Adaptive Sparsity over Key Sources for Video Editing), a training-free sparse attention framework that allocates computation independently for each query and key source. Specifically, for each query, QASK-Edit considers both the attention mass and approximation risk of each block. It then evaluates candidate routing thresholds against each key source's risk budget, choosing exact computation or approximations to dynamically adjust sparsity for each query. Extensive experiments on three video editing models demonstrate that QASK-Edit achieves up to $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup over dense attention pipeline while preserving both editing quality and unedited region fidelity. Furthermore, QASK-Edit generalizes directly to Reference-to-Video generation, delivering up to $1.36\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality.

2611.20565.tldr: Quantizes only the draft model's KV cache in speculative decoding to K4V4 (KIVI-style per-channel keys, per-token values), cutting draft cache memory 66% and total cache 24% across six model pairs with acceptance falling from 57.93% to 57.14%.
2611.20565.why: Relevant to efficient inference and quantized KV caches, which transfer to video diffusion transformers; the finding that key/value bit allocation depends on quantizer layout is a useful caution.
2611.20565.reason: KV cache quantization for efficient inference, though for LLM speculative decoding rather than video
2611.20565.qn: Sound but incremental: applies existing KIVI to draft cache; modest, expected result.
2611.20565.abs: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.

2611.20546.reason: Efficient rendering of structured 3DGS along camera trajectories, close to 3D reconstruction.
2611.20546.qn: Clear data-management framing for 3DGS trajectory rendering; gains need quantitative confirmation.
2611.20546.abs: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.

2611.20433.reason: Incremental 3D Gaussian reconstruction across time; close to 3D/4D reconstruction interests
2611.20433.qn: Clear incremental 3DGS update scheme with storage and depth gains
2611.20433.abs: Scene chronology aims to reconstruct a scene across visits separated by hours or days, during which objects may change in position, presence or shape. Such reconstruction must retain every earlier state, yet each revisit often provides only a few images. Storing a complete model for each visit duplicates the unchanged scene, whereas updating a single shared model alters earlier states. We present ReScene, which stores each visit as an immutable compact update, so that any earlier visit can be recovered exactly by applying the stored updates in order, without retaining past images. To localise each update, ReScene attributes the disagreement between the preceding reconstruction and the new images to individual Gaussians through their compositing weights. This attribution guides the suppression of outdated Gaussians and the refinement of persistent ones, while newly visible surfaces are initialised from learned multi-view depth. We also introduce Multi-State, a benchmark of non-rigid deformation and partial material removal, including synthetic scenes with ground-truth geometry. ReScene achieves quality higher than sequential 3DGS checkpointing with 2.5--4.8$\times$ less uncompressed history storage. At comparable PSNR, it also reduces foreground depth error by 3.2$\times$ relative to sequential ChronoGS, showing that accurate rendering does not necessarily imply accurate geometry. Code and benchmark are available at https://waychin-weiqin.github.io/ReScene/.

Luminosity-stratified dynamics give bright stars individual orbits supervised across image scales and carry faint populations with a velocity field estimated from optical flow. We further build a 4D dataset of eight galaxies from four cosmological simulations, on which Cosmos4D outperforms dynamic Gaussian baselines in both photometric quality and physical accuracy. With these advancements, we glimpse eight hundred million years of a galaxy's life in ninety-six frames.
